newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan OKs nine pct oil price hike from Jan 1.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan OKs nine pct oil price hike from Jan 1.

text.p: Taiwan's economics ministry said on Tuesday it had authorised Chinese Petroleum Corp, a state monopoly, to raise domestic petrol prices by nine percent to alleviate growing budgetary shortfalls.

A special ministry review panel that made the authorisation also agreed to let Chinese Petroleum raise local oil prices further -- but by no more than three percent -- after three months, a ministry official said.
Chinese Petroleum officials said they would put the initial increase into effect overnight.

"The rates will be effective starting at midnight tonight," a Chinese Petroleum official told reporters after a closed-door afternoon meeting at which a special ministry panel authorised the increases.
The oil monopoly has reported a November pre-tax loss of T$1.29 billion and a cumulative budget deficit of T$8.126 billion for the July-November period.
It has blamed the deficit mainly on world oil prices that were far higher than expected, saying it would need a 14 percent oil price increase to eliminate its current deficit.
"The price hike is purely to reflect the increase in the cost of oil purchases and has nothing to do with the company's operation efficiency," Chinese Petroleum said in a statement.
Chinese Petroleum's November oil import costs averaged US$22.13 per barrel, much higher than the budgeted US$15.26 per barrel, according to company figures.
Taiwan, almost totally dependent on foreign crude, imports more than 150 million barrels a year.
The monopoly's 95-octane petrol now sells for T$16.7 per litre (US$2.29 per gallon) at filling stations, including a T$0.2 per litre air-pollution surcharge.
The price will rise T$1.2 per litre on January 1.
Prices for diesel will rise T$0.9 per liter and those for fuel oil T$4.53 per litre.
